sentences.text: This Criminal Revision Petition is filed by the petitioners, being aggrieved by the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 25.09.2012 in C.C.No.42/2008 on the file of the Senior Civil Judge and J.M.F.C., at Gubbi and its confirmation judgment and order dated 27.03.2015 in Crl.A.No.157/2012 on the file of the II Additional District and Sessions Judge, Tumkur has filed this revision petition seeking to set aside the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below, wherein the petitioners / accused were convicted for the offences punishable under Section 498-A r/w Section 34 of Indian Penal Code (for short 'IPC').
2. The petitioners are the accused before the Trial Court and appellants before the Appellate Court.

Brief facts of the case are as under:
3.
It is the case of the prosecution that, accused No.1/petitioner No.1 was loving PW.2.
PW.2 was intending to marry accused No.1, however, he refused to marry her.
PW.2 brought to the notice of PW.3 and CW.6 about the love affair and PWs.7, 8, and CWs.12 and 13 have advised both of them and also instructed accused No.1 to marry PW.2.
It is further stated that the marriage of accused No.1 and PW.2 was performed on 19.06.2006 at Gubbi Sri Channabasaveshwara Temple by the elders and it was registered at Sub Registrar Office, Gubbi.

4. It is further stated that, after the marriage, PW.2 led her marital life in the house of the petitioners for one month happily, thereafter, she was thrown out of the matrimonial house and asked her to bring dowry in the form of cash of Rs.25,000/- and thus, she was being harassed, both mentally and physically.

A panchayat was conducted on 02.06.2007 in the presence of PWs.3, 4, 5,
and CW.6, in the house of accused No.1 and they advised accused No.1 to take care of PW.2 in the matrimonial house.
As per the said panchayat, PW.2 joined the matrimonial home.
However, on 05.06.2007, the accused No.1 assaulted PW.2 with his hands, demanding dowry, and asked her to bring money and threw her from the house.
Hence, PW.2 complained to the police.

The police have registered a case in Crime No.138/2007 for the offences under Sections 498-A r/w 34 of IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act (for short 'DP Act').
5.
To prove the case of the prosecution, the prosecution examined, in all, 16 witnesses as PWs.1 to 16 and marked 14 documents as Exhibits P1 to P14.
On the other hand, Ex.D1 was marked by the accused.

The Trial Court after appreciating both the oral and documentary evidence on record,
convicted petitioner No.1 for the offence under Section 498-A of IPC and sentenced him to undergo simple imprisonment for three years and also directed him to pay a fine of Rs.3,000/-, in default of payment of fine, he is ordered to undergo imprisonment for 9 months.

Similarly, accused No.2 was convicted for the offence under Section 498-A of IPC and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs.3,000/-, in default of the said fine amount, he was sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for six months.

Being aggrieved by the same, the Rajaiah vs The State Of Karnataka on 19 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34714055/

sentences.text: petitioners herein preferred an appeal before the Appellate Court, the Appellate Court confirmed the judgment of conviction rendered by the Trial Court.
Being aggrieved by the same, the petitioners have preferred this revision petition seeking to set aside the concurrent findings.
During the pendency of this revision petition, petitioner No.2 died on 07.03.2023, therefore, the case against petitioner No.2 stands abated.

6. Heard Shri A H Bhagavan, learned counsel for the petitioner No.1 and Shri Rahul Rai.K., learned High Court Government Pleader for the respondent - State.
7.

It is the submission of the learned counsel for the petitioners that, the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below in convicting petitioner No.1 require to be set aside since the findings are perverse, arbitrary, and erroneous for the reason that the said findings are opposed to the law and facts.

8. It is further submitted that PWs 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8 are all related witnesses, their evidence should have been considered by the Courts below with due diligence and should have been scrutinized properly since, they are interested witnesses.
However the Courts below failed to take note of the said fact and recorded the conviction which is erroneous.
9. It is further submitted that merely sending PW.2 to her parent's house due to some petty reasons may not amount to cruelty.

The Trial Court and the Appellate Court even though concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the provisions under Sections 3 and 4 of the DP Act, the conviction of petitioner No.1 in respect of offence under Section 498-A of IPC appears to be erroneous and said the conviction is unsustainable.
The Trial Court and the Appellate Court ignored in considering this aspect resulting in recording the conviction.
Hence, the same is required to be set aside.
Making such submission, learned counsel for the petitioners seeks to set aside the concurrent findings recorded by both the Courts below.

10. Per contra, learned High Court Government Pleader (for short 'HCGP') vehemently justifies the concurrent findings and submits that the evidence of PWs.2, 3, 4, 5, and 8 are relevant, though they are the related witnesses, in the matrimonial cases, their evidence has to be considered as that of other evidence.
They are the best witnesses to speak about cruelty and harassment in matrimonial issues.
The Trial Court and the Appellate Court rightly convicted for the offence under Section 498-A r/w 34 of IPC.

There is no infirmity or illegality in the findings of the Trial Court, therefore,
the petition deserves to be dismissed.
Having submitted thus, learned HCGP prays to dismiss the petition.

11. Having heard the rival contentions urged by the learned counsels for the respective parties and also perused the concurrent findings of the Courts below, the points that arise for my consideration are:
i) Whether the concurrent findings recorded by both the Courts below in convicting the petitioner No.1 for the offence under Sections 498-A r/w 34 of IPC is sustainable?

sentences.text: ii) Whether the petitioner No.1 has made out grounds to interfere with the concurrent findings recorded by both the Courts below for conviction?

12. This Court being a Revisional Court, having regard to the scope and ambit envisaged to appreciate the facts and law, it is necessary to have a cursory look upon the evidence and also the law, to ascertain as to whether any illegality or perversity or error committed by the Courts below in recording the conviction.

13. To avoid the repetition of the facts, it is stated that, PW.2 is the wife of accused No.1, their marriage was performed at the intervention of the elders since accused No.1 was not interested in marrying PW.2.
It is also noticed that, PW.2 was thrown out of the house of accused No.1 asking her to bring dowry of Rs.25,000/- from her parents' house.
Panchayat was held and accused No.1 was advised to look after PW.2 without any harassment.

14. On careful reading of the findings of the Trial Court, the Trial Court acquitted the petitioners for the offence under Sections 3 and 4 of the DP Act and convicted the petitioners for the offence under Section 498-A of IPC.
15.

Now it is relevant to refer the provision under Section 498-A of IPC, which reads thus:
"498A. Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.--Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman,
subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.--For the purpose of this section, "cruelty" means-- (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand."
16.

On reading of the above-said provision, it makes it clear that to constitute an offence, the woman must be subjected to cruelty in connection with the demand of dowry or any other reason stated in sub-clause (a) of section 498 - A of IPC, the said cruelty must be of such nature that, it has driven the woman to commit suicide.
17.
Now, it is relevant to refer to the legal proposition of law on this point.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of UNDAVALLI NARAYANA RAO v. STATE OF A.P.1, paragraph Nos.14 to 22,
held thus:-

The provisions of Section 498-A IPC read as under:
"498-A. Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty.--Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman,
subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
Explanation.--For the purposes of this section, 'cruelty' means-- (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause (2009) 14 SCC 588 - 10 - grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand."
15.
"Cruelty" has been defined by the Explanation added to the section itself.
The basic ingredients of Section 498-A IPC are cruelty and harassment.

The elements of cruelty so far as clause (a) is concerned, have been classified as follows:
(i) any "wilful" conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide; or (ii) any "wilful" conduct which is likely to cause grave injury to the woman; or (iii) any "wilful" act which is likely to cause danger to life, limb or health, whether physical or mental of the woman.

For the purpose of clause (b) the essential ingredients are as under:
(i) the harassment of a married woman - 11 - (ii) with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet the unlawful demand of dowry or for any property or valuable security or on account of her failure or failure of any person related to her to meet such a demand.
Therefore, it is evident that the charge under Section 498-A can be brought home if the essential ingredients either in clause (a) or (b) or both are found duly established.

In S. Hanumantha Rao v. S. Ramani this Court considered the meaning of cruelty in the context of the provisions under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 and observed that : (SCC p. 624,
para 8) "8. ... Mental cruelty broadly means, when either party causes mental pain, agony or suffering of such a magnitude that it severs the bond between the wife and the husband and as a result of which it becomes impossible for the party who has suffered to live with the other party.

entities.text: S. Hanumantha Rao v. S. Ramani
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In other words, the party who has committed wrong is - 12 - not expected to live with the other party."

17. In V. Bhagat v. D. Bhagat this Court, while dealing with the issue of cruelty in the context of Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, observed as under :
(SCC pp. 347 & 349, paras 16-17) "16. ...
It is not necessary to prove that the mental cruelty is such as to cause injury to the health of the petitioner.

While arriving at such conclusion, regard must be had to the social status, educational level of the parties,
the society they move in, the possibility or otherwise of the parties ever living together in case they are already living apart and all other relevant facts and circumstances which it is neither possible nor desirable to set out exhaustively.
What is cruelty in one case may not amount to cruelty in another case.
It is a matter to be determined in each case having regard to the facts and circumstances of that case.
If it is a case of accusations and allegations, regard must also be had to the context in which they were made.
... The context and the set- up in which the word 'cruelty' has been used in the section, seems to us, that intention is not a necessary element in cruelty.
That word has to be understood in the ordinary sense of the term in matrimonial affairs.
If the intention to harm, harass or hurt could be inferred by the nature of the conduct or brutal act complained of, cruelty could be easily established.

But the absence of intention should not make any difference in the case, if by ordinary sense in human affairs, the act complained of could otherwise be regarded as cruelty."
18.
In Mohd. Hoshan v. State of A.P. this Court while dealing with the similar issue held that mental or physical torture should be "continuously" practised by the accused on the wife.

entities.text: Mohd. Hoshan v. State of A.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Court further observed as under : (SCC p. 418, para 6) "6.
Whether one spouse has been guilty of cruelty to the other is essentially a question of fact.

The impact of complaints, accusations or taunts on a person amounting to cruelty depends on various factors like the sensitivity of the individual victim concerned, the social - 14 - Rajaiah vs The State Of Karnataka on 19 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34714055/
6  background, the environment,
 education, etc.
Further, mental cruelty varies from person to person depending on the intensity of sensitivity and the degree of courage or endurance to withstand such mental cruelty.

In other words, each case has to be decided on its own facts to decide whether the mental cruelty was established or not."
19.

In Raj Rani v. State (Delhi Admn this Court held that while considering the case of cruelty in the context of the provisions of Section 498-A IPC, the court must examine that allegations/accusations must be of a very grave nature and should be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

20. In Sushil Kumar Sharma v.
Union of India this Court explained the distinction of cruelty as provided under Sections 306 and 498-A IPC observing that under Section 498-A cruelty committed by the husband or his relation drive woman to commit suicide, etc. while under Section 306 IPC, suicide is abetted and intended.

. In Girdhar Shankar Tawade v.
State of Maharashtr this Court held that "cruelty" has to be understood having a specific statutory meaning provided in Section 498-A IPC and there should be a case of continuous state of affairs of torture by one to another.

sentences.text: 22. In Explanation (b) there is absence of physical injury but it includes coercive harassment for demand of dowry, etc.
Therefore the aforesaid provisions deal with patent and latent acts of the husband or his family members.
But both are equally serious in terms of the provisions of the statute.

The provisions of Section 498-A IPC were introduced by an amendment to curb the harassment of a woman by her husband and or his family members, for demand of dowry, etc.
under the garb of fulfilment of the customary obligations."

On careful reading of the provision and also the dictum of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, it makes it clear that to constitute an offence, the woman must be subjected to cruelty either in connection with general cruelty or in connection with demand of dowry.
The said cruelty must be such of nature that the situation creates the woman to commit suicide.
Taking into consideration, the above proposition of law, it is required to examine the facts of the present case.
The evidence of PW.2 discloses that the marriage was forcible marriage.
It was performed at the intervention of the elders of the village.
The said marriage was performed in the temple and the same was registered in the Sub-Registrar Office at Gubbi.
PW.2 stated in her complaint that, she was subjected to cruelty in connection with the demand of dowry in the form of amount of Rs.25,000/-.

When she could not bring the said amount, she stated to have been thrown Rajaiah vs The State Of Karnataka on 19 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34714055/
7 out of the matrimonial home.

sentences.text: However, it is noted here that, the Trial Court acquitted Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, for which no appeal was filed by PW.2 or the State.
It is needless to say that, mere trivial issues in the matrimonial house cannot be construed as cruelty and harassment.
19. In the present case, PW.2 has hardly stayed in the matrimonial home for about one month from the date of marriage and she was stated to have been thrown out of the matrimonial home.
In the instant case, the averments of the complaint and the evidence of PW.2 and her relatives indicate that no such cruelty and harassment had been caused to PW.2.

It appears from the evidence that there was a forcible - 17 - marriage between accused No.1 and PW.2 and there might be a difference of opinion between the husband and wife, however, it cannot be construed that, PW.2 has been subjected to cruelty at matrimonial house.
20.
It is needless to say that, the Trial Court has rightly acquitted the petitioners for the offences under Sections 3 and 4 of the D.P. Act.
However, as per the averments of the complaint, PW.2 was thrown out of the house in connection with the demand for dowry in the form of an amount.
The Trial Court and the Appellate Court failed to take note of the law on this point and recorded the conviction, which is perverse, illegal and the same is liable to be set aside.
Therefore, interference of this Court by exercising the Revisional jurisdiction is justified.

 Point No.(i) - "Negative"

21. In the light of the observations made above, the points that arose for my consideration are answered as under:-
